comm.t: Medhas, the sage whose hermitage Suratha found (1.10), begins his answer to the question of 1.40–45. From here the ṛṣi is the narrator of the Goddess’s deeds; his answer runs to the end of the text.

samasa.sense: in the sphere of what the senses grasp
samasa.alt: Also read as a karmadhāraya, विषयः एव गोचरः ‘the field that is the object’; the sense is the same. गोचर is literally ‘where cattle graze’, then any range or province.

morph.note: With a genitive, ‘to be’ means ‘to have’: समस्तस्य जन्तोः ज्ञानम् अस्ति ‘every creature has knowledge’.
Genitive singular of an u-stem: guṇa of the stem vowel + -ः (जन्तु → जन्तोः).

mantras.anvaya_en: A simple existential sentence: possessor in the genitive, sphere in the locative, subject ज्ञानम्, verb अस्ति.
mantras.lit: There is knowledge of every creature in the range of sense-objects.
mantras.tr: Every living creature has knowledge in the realm of the senses.

comm.t: Medhas begins by granting the king’s premise in a limited way: yes, there is knowledge — but the knowledge every creature has, knowledge of sense-objects.

The word picks up the king’s विषय (1.44). The text will distinguish this ordinary knowing from the knowledge that frees, which it calls the supreme विद्या and identifies with the Goddess herself (1.57).

mantras.anvaya: (हे) महाभाग, विषयः च एवं पृथक् पृथक् याति च। केचित् प्राणिनः दिवा अन्धाः, तथा अपरे रात्रौ अन्धाः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A general statement (the object reaches each being differently), then two examples in nominal sentences (the verb ‘are’ understood).
mantras.lit: And the sense-object, O blessed one, reaches (creatures) thus, severally. Some creatures are blind by day; likewise others are blind at night.
mantras.tr: And the world of objects, blessed one, reaches each creature in its own way. Some creatures are blind by day, others blind by night,
mantras.tr_note: ‘creatures’ in the first sentence is supplied; the Sanskrit says only that the object ‘goes’ severally.

comm.t: Medhas illustrates: knowledge of objects is not uniform. What a creature can know depends on its nature — some see only by night, some only by day. The text names no species.
The point prepares the next step: if knowing objects were what made a being wise, the animals would be wise too (1.49–50). The knowledge the king has is real but of this ordinary kind.

samasa.sense: who see alike by day and night

morph.note: Accusative neuter of सत्य used as an adverb of concession: ‘true, (men) are knowers’ — answered by किं तु ‘but’.
Adverbial accusative of केवल ‘alone’: न हि केवलम् ‘not (they) alone, indeed’.

mantras.anvaya: केचित् प्राणिनः दिवा तथा रात्रौ तुल्यदृष्टयः। मनुजाः सत्यं ज्ञानिनः, किं तु ते केवलं न हि (ज्ञानिनः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three nominal clauses with ‘are’ understood: the third example of creatures, a concession about men, and its correction.
mantras.lit: Some creatures are of equal sight by day and likewise at night. Men are truly possessed of knowledge; but they indeed are not the only ones.
mantras.tr: and some see alike by day and by night. Human beings have knowledge, it is true — but they are not alone in having it.

comm.t: Medhas completes the list (blind by day, blind by night, seeing in both) and turns it on the king’s claim to be a ‘knower’: humans do know, but knowledge of this kind is shared with all creatures.

samasa.vigraha: पशवश्च पक्षिणश्च मृगाश्च पशुपक्षिमृगाः; पशुपक्षिमृगाः आदयः येषां ते
samasa.literal: those of whom cattle, birds and wild beasts are the first

morph.note: पक्षिन् ‘bird’ drops its final n inside the compound (पक्षि-). पशु is the domestic animal, मृग the wild one.
Pronominal nominative plural in -e (सर्व, like अपरे in 1.48).

mantras.anvaya: यतः हि पशुपक्षिमृगादयः सर्वे ज्ञानिनः (सन्ति)। मनुष्याणां च तत् ज्ञानम् (अस्ति), यत् तेषां मृगपक्षिणाम् (अस्ति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal clause (यतः …) and a relative pair (तत् … यत्): men’s knowledge is the same as that which belongs to beasts and birds.
mantras.lit: For all — cattle, birds, wild beasts and the rest — are possessed of knowledge. And men have that knowledge which those beasts and birds (have);
mantras.tr: for every creature — cattle, birds, wild beasts and the rest — has knowledge. And the knowledge men have is the same as that of beasts and birds,

comm.t: The argument reaches its point: as far as knowledge of objects goes, humans and animals are on a level. The king’s ‘knowing’ (1.42, 1.44) is of this kind, and so it cannot by itself free him.
A modern reading: the sage is not belittling the king. He is moving the question from how much one knows to what one is bound by — the subject of the next three verses.
